The Priest in his Boots

This is the version in Breandan Breathnac’s Ceol Rince na hEirreann cd2
Michael Tubridy publishes Dan Fury’s setting in his book on Traditional step dancing (Piper’s Club, Dublin)
I have seen it mentioned as a Wexford Mummers dance

The Priest in his Boots

My wife insists that “Boots” is a reference to prophylactic devices. I feel compelled to pass on this outré observation on her behalf.

↳ Posted by David Levine on February 19th, 2007.

Can be found in the Gunn Book (1865) and still popular in Fermanagh. Big John McManus plays in G and then in A. Very effective. There is also a specific dance for this tune

↳ Posted by The Archivist on November 12th, 2009.

Oops. Big John McManus and others in Fermanagh play this tune in G then D (not A)

↳ Posted by The Archivist on January 21st, 2010.

This is an old Clare setting I got from Ben Power, who got both the tune and its sean-nós set dance from James Keane.

Imo it’s a different setting of the same tune. It’s a common dancing tune, someone mentioned above that it was a Wexford Mummers dance - it is still used in Fermanagh for the Mummers. They play it in 2 keys. Nice clip, thanks for sharing.

The Priest In His Boots, X:8

This version is close to the one added by Ebonian up there.
It’s the O’Neill version, accordingly to the cover of the self produced CD “For the Sake of Old Decency”, recorded in 1996 by Hervé Cantal, a nice French flute player, joined on this recording by some other French musicians. It’s the 2nd tune of a set of two jigs (which starts with a setting of “John Naughton’s”, https://thesession.org/tunes/23413).

↳ Posted by G.Ryckeboer on August 9th, 2023.

Re: The Priest In His Boots / Tivoli

Tivoli is name given to setting in D in RMC (#463). Ryan’s setting in G, #406, is called The Priest in His Boots.

↳ Posted by brailsford on August 16th, 2023.

Re: The Priest In His Boots

This tune can be found in Thompson’s Twenty Four Country Dances for the Year 1791 under the title “The Welch Jig”.

↳ Posted by Nigel Gatherer on November 3rd, 2023.

The Priest In His Boots, X:9

Following the idea of the first version in D found at the top of this page (submitted 22 years before), this is the version given by Breandan Breathnach in his third “Ceol Rince na hEireann” cuid3 (RCE3 #8 p5). By the way it seems to exist an other page in this site about that tune, so I precise that this version is pretty close to https://thesession.org/tunes/1991 #1 as far as notes about this version say that it is (also) coming from the playing of the flute player Paddy Taylor. There are slighty differences in the phrasing and grace notes.

↳ Posted by velay-b on October 9th, 2024.

The Priest In His Boots, X:10

I see @velay-b added a setting earlier, coincidently I was transcribing my setting just a couple of hours ago. I play this on Lowland / Border pipes and my setting is based on that in James Oswald’s Caledonian Pocket Companion volume 10 from 1758 where it is called ‘The Irish Lilt’.

↳ Posted by bagpie on October 9th, 2024.

The Priest And His Boots, X:11

This setting is based on the playing of Matt and Joe Cunningham of Headford, Co. Galway. The dance of the same name has 5 figures. Matt plays the tune (AABB) 5 times through, plus an 8 bar A part introduction (168 bars total).

↳ Posted by Shawn Cassady on November 17th, 2024.

Re: The Priest In His Boots

Seems to be a very similar tune to Mopsi Dôn, a tune submitted elsewhere on this site. This would tie in with Nigel Gatherer’s post regarding ‘The Welch Jig’, and the connection has been noted on the submission for Mopsi Dôn.
More transcription here:
https://tunearch.org/wiki/Mopsy%27s_Tune_(the_Old_Way)
